implementation_notes: EF Core maps the aggregate as one unit: `OwnsMany`/`[Owned]` make the parts owned entity types that 'cannot exist without' the owner, private fields are mapped with `HasField` (values are then read and written without going through the property), and reference owned types share the owner's table by default; owned collections such as `OwnsMany` normally use a separate table unless configured otherwise. The root exposes `IReadOnlyList<OrderLine>` over a private `List<OrderLine>` and mutates it only through methods; a `DbContext` tracks the root and its owned parts, while the application scopes `SaveChanges` and its transaction to one command.
pitfalls: A navigation exposed only as `IReadOnlyList<OrderLine>` with no mapped backing field loads nothing: configure the field (`HasField("_lines")` or the `_`/`_camel` convention) so EF can materialize the collection.
`AsReadOnly()` is a wrapper around the live list - handing out the backing `List<OrderLine>` (or a method that does) lets callers bypass AddLine.
Owned types cannot have their own `DbSet`: needing one means the concept was modelled as its own aggregate, and querying children directly is exactly the bypass the boundary forbids.
Calling `SaveChanges` after mutating two aggregates in one method spans two consistency boundaries; publish a domain event and commit the second aggregate separately.

variants.name: Persistence-ignorant POCO aggregate with an explicit repository
variants.implementation_notes: Without an ORM the root is a plain class (or a record for the value parts) with a private `List<OrderLine>`, a read-only projection and validating methods, and the unit of work is an explicit `IDbTransaction` around a hand-written repository that writes root and children together. Choose this when the domain assembly must not reference EF Core - the C# variant of the persistence-ignorant model, and the one that keeps invariants testable without a DbContext.
pitfalls: `IReadOnlyList<T>` is a compile-time view: a caller who casts back to List<T> mutates the aggregate, so return a copy when the value crosses an assembly boundary.
No change tracker means the repository must compare and write children itself - forgetting to delete removed lines leaves orphan rows that later violate the invariant on load.
Without EF's backing-field materialization the constructor is the only creation path; a serializer or DI framework that sets properties directly can produce an invariant-violating instance.
